question.problem: Find the principal $7$th root of unity.
question.worked_solution:
Let $z$ be a $7$th root of unity. This means that 

$$
{z}^{7}=1.
$$

First, we express the complex number $1$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta }.$ Notice that $|1|=1$ and $\operatorname{arg}⁡(1)=0.$ Hence, 

$$
1={e}^{\text{i}(0+2k\pi )}={e}^{2k\pi \text{i}},
$$

where $k$ is an integer. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{7}={e}^{2k\pi \text{i}}\,⟹\,z=({e}^{2k\pi \text{i}})^{1/7}={e}^{2k\pi \text{i}/7}.\end{aligned}
$$

The principal root corresponds to $k=1,$ and is therefore equal to ${e}^{2\pi \text{i}/7}.$

- one of the roots is $1,$ corresponding to the point $(1,0)$ on the complex plane,

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980994/assets/b575a8b3c4830aa48586b457b45f76ca8df49ecf8036df720f66aaddc857bdaf.png)

Find the root of unity highlighted in the diagram above.
question.worked_solution:
The $n$th roots of unity lie at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed inside the unit circle in the complex plane. One of the vertices of this regular $n$-gon must lie at the point $(1,0).$

Since there are $6$ points in our diagram, we need to find a $6$th root of unity.

First, we express the complex number $1$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta }.$ Notice that $|1|=1$ and $\operatorname{arg}⁡(1)=0.$ Hence, 

$$
1={e}^{\text{i}(0+2k\pi )}={e}^{2k\pi \text{i}},
$$

where $k$ is an integer. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{6}={e}^{2k\pi \text{i}}\,⟹\,z=({e}^{2k\pi \text{i}})^{1/6}={e}^{k\pi \text{i}/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the index $k$ of our root of unity, we enumerate the roots in the diagram counter-clockwise, starting with the root at $(1,0)$ corresponding to $k=0,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980994/assets/34a3bb77a9765cd806a047ad42a7f0719201effdd46659efe7ffd1a94a051910.png)

 

So, the required root corresponds to $k=5.$ Substituting this into the expression for roots, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}_{5}={e}^{(5)\pi \text{i}/3}={e}^{5\pi \text{i}/3}\end{aligned}
$$
